clinicalPearls: Primary hyperparathyroidism (pHPT) and malignancy are the two most common causes of hypercalcemia; the diagnostic split hinges on the PTH level (Harrison 22e p.3271).

pHPT is almost always a benign neoplastic disorder of the parathyroids (adenoma or hyperplasia) producing PTH that is not appropriately suppressed by the elevated calcium; parathyroid carcinoma is a rare cause (Harrison 22e p.3271).

In hypercalcemia, an elevated or 'inappropriately normal' PTH with elevated calcium and low/low-normal phosphorus is almost always pHPT; because of PTH's phosphaturic action, pHPT hypercalcemia is often accompanied by low/frankly low serum phosphate (Harrison 22e p.3271).

A suppressed PTH in the face of hypercalcemia means the process is independent of the parathyroid glands and is most often malignancy; many solid tumors secrete PTHrP, which mimics PTH at its receptor on bone and kidney (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Hypercalcemia from lymphoma or granulomatous disease (e.g., sarcoidosis, tuberculosis) is driven by extrarenal macrophage CYP27B1 conversion of 25(OH)D to 1,25(OH)2D; in such cases 1,25(OH)2D is increased or inappropriately normal (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Classic chronic hypercalcemia (months to years, fluctuating between high-normal and just above normal) is most often pHPT or FHH, occasionally multiple myeloma; malignancy-associated hypercalcemia usually has a more acute course (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Mild hypercalcemia (10.5-11.9 mg/dL) is largely asymptomatic; symptoms ('stones, bones, groans') include nephrolithiasis, reduced bone density / bone pain or pathologic fractures with long-standing hyperparathyroidism, constipation/nausea/vomiting/anorexia/peptic ulcer/pancreatitis, plus fatigue, proximal weakness, hyporeflexia, and neuropsychiatric changes (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Hypocalcemia is differentiated by whether PTH is low (hypoparathyroidism) or high (secondary hyperparathyroidism); a low or 'inappropriately low' PTH with hypocalcemia establishes hypoparathyroidism, whereas an elevated PTH points to the vitamin D axis or primary small-bowel calcium malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.3271).

In adults, hypoparathyroidism most commonly results from inadvertent damage to all four parathyroid glands during thyroid or parathyroid surgery; autoimmune endocrinopathy accounts for about a quarter of cases (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Neuromuscular irritability of hypocalcemia is detected by Chvostek's sign (perioral twitch on tapping the facial nerve) and the more specific Trousseau's sign (carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic for 3 min); paresthesias of fingers, toes, and circumoral region are typical (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Because PTH is the main minute-by-minute defense against hypocalcemia, hypoparathyroidism can produce profound, life-threatening hypocalcemia, whereas vitamin D deficiency causes less severe hypocalcemia since the parathyroids mount a compensatory PTH rise (at the expense of bone) (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Impaired PTH secretion may be secondary to magnesium deficiency (via intracellular effects); hypomagnesemic hypocalcemia will not correct until magnesium is repleted (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Hungry bone syndrome after parathyroidectomy is a recognized cause of post-operative hypocalcemia with high PTH (Harrison 22e p.3271).
harrison.pathophysiology: Extracellular calcium is held in a narrow range (~8.5-10.5 mg/dL) by feedback among the parathyroids, kidney, bone, and intestine. A fall in ECF calcium is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on parathyroid chief cells, triggering PTH release; PTH increases bone calcium resorption, distal-tubule reabsorption of filtered calcium, and renal proximal-tubule 1,25(OH)2D production, and 1,25(OH)2D in turn raises intestinal calcium absorption. Hypercalcemia arises from derangements of this loop: PTH-dependent overproduction (pHPT due to adenoma/hyperplasia, rarely carcinoma; tertiary hyperparathyroidism; ectopic PTH; FHH and CaSR-altering states such as lithium), or PTH-independent mechanisms (PTHrP-secreting tumors, lytic skeletal metastases, extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D production in granulomatous disease/lymphoma, vitamin D intoxication, increased bone resorption from thyrotoxicosis/Paget's/immobilization, and calcium overload e.g. milk-alkali). Hypocalcemia results from low PTH (hypoparathyroidism: surgical, autoimmune, infiltrative, genetic, CaSR-activating, or magnesium-related) or high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency, renal failure, intestinal malabsorption, or PTH resistance/pseudohypoparathyroidism). Low calcium increases neuromuscular irritability (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disease - 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcemia
Lymphoma (B cell, cutaneous T cell/Sezary) - extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D
Thyrotoxicosis, Paget's disease, immobilization - increased bone resorption mimicking parathyroid hypercalcemia
Thiazides, lithium, vitamin A, foscarnet, teriparatide, aromatase inhibitors - drug-induced hypercalcemia
Acute pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, burns - hypocalcemia from tissue injury / hyperphosphatemia
Respiratory or metabolic alkalosis - hypocalcemia from increased calcium binding to albumin
additionalInvestigations: Total serum calcium with serum albumin to calculate corrected calcium (add 0.8 mg/dL per 1.0 g/dL albumin below 4.0; subtract when albumin is high)
Intact PTH by two-site assay - the key second test that separates PTH-dependent from PTH-independent disorders
Serum phosphorus (low/low-normal in pHPT; elevated in some hypocalcemic states)
Serum magnesium (hypo- or severe hypermagnesemia impairs PTH)
Serum 25(OH)D - useful in both hyper- and hypocalcemia to assess vitamin D stores
Serum 1,25(OH)2D - useful in hypercalcemia (increased/inappropriately normal in granulomatous disease or lymphoma) and suspected vitamin D resistance
PTHrP level when hypercalcemia of malignancy is suspected with suppressed PTH
Serum free light chains / SPEP-UPEP with immunofixation to exclude multiple myeloma
Calcium/creatinine clearance ratio (<0.01 suggests FHH); 24-hour urinary fractional calcium excretion (>0.02 supports pHPT)
Genetic sequencing of CASR, GNA11, AP2S1 for definitive FHH diagnosis when urine studies are inconclusive; genetic testing for syndromic/hereditary pHPT (MEN, CDC73)
ECG (hypercalcemia: bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc; hypocalcemia: QTc prolongation)
redFlags: Moderate-to-severe hypercalcemia (>=12-14 mg/dL) with progressive lethargy, stupor, or coma
Hypercalcemia with acute renal failure and volume depletion from polyuria
Hypercalcemic ECG changes: bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc
Severe hypocalcemia causing seizures, carpopedal spasm, bronchospasm, or laryngospasm
Hypocalcemic QTc prolongation with risk of ventricular tachyarrhythmia (Torsade) and sudden death
Tetany (positive Trousseau's sign / carpal spasm) signaling impending neuromuscular crisis
New severe hypocalcemia after thyroid or parathyroid neck surgery (damage to all four glands), especially in patients with prior malabsorption
Syndromic pHPT with a jaw tumor (CDC73 mutation) carrying ~30% lifetime risk of parathyroid carcinoma
harrison.prognosis: Mild, asymptomatic hypercalcemia (commonly pHPT detected incidentally in settings with routine calcium screening) carries a benign short-term course, whereas advanced pHPT can cause severe skeletal disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica). Hypoparathyroidism, because PTH is the chief minute-by-minute defense against hypocalcemia, can be profound, debilitating, and life-threatening, while vitamin D-deficiency hypocalcemia is typically milder owing to compensatory PTH secretion (at the expense of bone). Severe hypercalcemia (coma, renal failure, arrhythmia) and severe hypocalcemia (seizures, laryngospasm, Torsade) are medical emergencies (Harrison 22e p.3271).
pitfalls: Failing to correct calcium for albumin before launching a workup - low albumin can mask true hypercalcemia and falsely suggest hypocalcemia (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Mistaking FHH for pHPT: FHH can present with mildly elevated PTH and hypercalcemia, but parathyroid surgery is ineffective; a calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 and family history of mild asymptomatic hypercalcemia or repeated failed neck surgeries should prompt CASR/GNA11/AP2S1 testing (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Overlooking lithium therapy, which raises the CaSR set point and can cause hyperparathyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Not repleting magnesium in hypocalcemia: hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and the hypocalcemia will not correct until magnesium is restored (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Chvostek's sign is nonspecific - present in ~10% of normal individuals; Trousseau's sign is the more definitive marker of neuromuscular irritability (Harrison 22e p.3271).

Attributing hypercalcemia of immobilization solely to bed rest - an unrecognized resorptive process (pHPT, Paget's, myeloma) may be the real driver, especially in older patients (Harrison 22e p.3271).
When tetany accompanies alkalosis, a second cause of impaired calcium homeostasis is usually present (Harrison 22e p.3271).
Ectopic PTH secretion, unlike pHPT, does not fluctuate with correction of calcium because it is not under CaSR control (Harrison 22e p.3271).
harrison.severityClassification: Hypercalcemia severity (Harrison 22e p.3271): mild 10.5-11.9 mg/dL (largely asymptomatic); moderate >=12-14 mg/dL; severe >=14 mg/dL (progressive lethargy, stupor, coma, prominent GI symptoms, acute renal failure). Hypocalcemia severity ranges from asymptomatic (mild/chronic) to moderate-severe with paresthesias, positive Chvostek's/Trousseau's signs, through severe with seizures, carpopedal spasm, broncho-/laryngospasm, and QTc prolongation with arrhythmia risk.
management: Treat symptomatic or severe hypercalcaemia acutely with isotonic saline rehydration, an intravenous bisphosphonate or denosumab, and calcitonin for rapid effect

Direct definitive therapy at the cause: parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism, tumour-directed treatment for malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia, and corticosteroids for 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin-D-mediated granulomatous or lymphoma-related hypercalcaemia
Use the calcimimetic cinacalcet to lower calcium in inoperable primary hyperparathyroidism or parathyroid carcinoma
Manage hypocalcaemia and hypoparathyroidism with oral calcium and activated vitamin D such as alfacalcidol or calcitriol, correcting any coexisting hypomagnesaemia
Recognise familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia and manage it conservatively, avoiding unnecessary parathyroid surgery
Withhold or review aggravating agents such as lithium and thiazide diuretics
Monitor serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium and renal function during treatment, with surveillance for renal and skeletal end-organ effects
